after.name: Question 1
after.worked_solution:
Let's recall the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${sin}^{2}$ term: 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta =1-2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta 
$$

Letting $\theta =\frac{x}{2}$, we have

$$
1-2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{x}{2})=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (1-2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{x}{2}))\text{d}x & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
Here, we use the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta $ term, given by

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta =2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -1.
$$

 

Rearranging, we have

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta +1).
$$

Letting $\theta =\frac{x}{2},$ we have

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{x}{2})=\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x+1).
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{x}{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x+1)\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int (\operatorname{cos}⁡x+1)\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+x)+C.\end{aligned}
$$
